The previous paragraph describes the soul as one containing many powers. This paragraph describes many powers gathered in one soul. The soul has all these powers without becoming many beings.

One might object that in thought we perceive mental images of colors and sounds, not actual sight and hearing. The reply is that “sight” here means the presence of light and color to the soul with the same vividness as when the eye sees them. One may call this imagination instead; the disagreement is about the name.

If the shapes of the organs depend on the powers' structures, the human powers lead to a circle in the explanation. The power of sight is ready only after the eye and the crossing of the optic nerves have formed, yet those forms are said to depend on the power of sight.
This point applies not only to the human and animal powers but to every power that receives something. Readiness to receive something near always depends on a form already present.
The point is that forms and powers have stages. Each earlier form helps prepare the matter for the one that follows, and that later form is the shadow of a higher power.
The heart is an example of the chief organ, not the only one. It is like the trunk of a tree, with the other organs as its branches.
A better example may be the way a simple intellect contains, in a unified way, the many intellects that flow from it.
The union meant here is that all things are contained in the simple reality in a higher, unified way.

These are the higher patterns or sources of kinds. They are complete beings with no further stage to reach, so they do not move from their station. Because they encompass lower levels, the particular forms below them descend and take shape. In this sense, the universal patterns themselves do not descend; their weaker forms do.
The partial form is the same reality in a weaker degree, just as the universal reality is the same in a stronger degree.
“Every soul” is meant generally, as in the verse “There is no creature that moves on the earth or bird that flies with its wings” (Qur'an 6:38).

Just as Israfil and his partial forms breathe spirit into matter, they also clothe matter in forms. For example, matter loses the form of chyle through a partial form of Azrael and receives the form of chyme through a partial form of Israfil.

Some powers are immaterial in themselves; others are bodily only through their effects. The latter are not fully free of matter. If Azrael is counted among the four great angels, he should also be named here with his partial forms; the author appears to include him in the phrase “the same applies to all powers.”

Natural philosophers place the animal soul in the brain because it branches into powers of perception and movement, both of which are there. The human soul itself has no bodily location; the author says only that its rule is in the brain. Another animal power governs the heart and arteries through the spirit within them, as explained later.
The pronoun refers to all the powers, not just to the human power. It could refer to practical intellect if “human power” is meant here as the practical intellect, which serves the theoretical one.

If seeing all things in the soul means that many things exist in it in a unified way, they exist there without parts. If it means that many separate powers are one in the soul, they are one because being is primary: what makes them different is the same existence that they share. Each is also a mirror of the simple self, which contains all things without becoming many. As the Persian verse says: “When we sent Adam out, we laid our beauty across the plain.”

The soul is a substance because the perceiver must exist in itself; an accident exists only in its subject, and so cannot perceive in its own right. The soul is sacred and free of matter because, if it existed only in matter, it would not perceive. The same reasoning shows that it cannot decay.

In the upward journey, the human being once stood at the level of prime matter: it was not yet a particular thing in actuality, though it held the potential for later forms. The verse describes a stage the human being passed through. The commentator also suggests a stage before creation, in God's knowledge, where the human being did not exist on its own; only God and His knowledge existed. The fixed realities of things have no independent existence there, and even less so at the beginning of their descent into the world.

The author builds this argument on the real bond between soul and body. A bond of being brings some kind of unity: if one exists for the other, it is a level of the other's existence. If the body is an accident, like a color, it exists in its subject. If body and soul are both substances, as matter and form are, they are higher and lower levels of one being. The stronger being contains the weaker, but does not erase the forms below it. This is an ordered relation, not two complete beings standing side by side.

The commentator offers a further explanation of the union between knower and known. Things in the external world and things in the mind are two forms of one reality. For something to exist in sight does not mean the eye is one thing and the visible object another, joined like a container and its contents. It means that the thing exists in a way that can be seen. In the same way, something existing in the mind is a way the soul exists; it is not a separate thing placed inside it. This is not just a comparison: both are forms of existence. If matter and form are one being, the union of the knower and known becomes clear. Alexander of Aphrodisias is said to have explained it in this way.

If each soul joined the whole Active Intellect, each would know what the others know. If each joined only a part, the Active Intellect would be divided. The answer is that the intellect exists in itself and also in each soul; the soul joins the way it exists in the soul, not the way it exists in itself.

The objections to the union of knower and known were answered in the First Journey. The author's own proof for this point is not complete. A better basis is the real bond between a power and what it can do. If an intelligible form has weaker existence than the knower, it is one of the knower's states, like an accident in its subject. If it has stronger existence, the knower is one of its levels, like an effect depends on its cause. This is especially clear of second matter in relation to its form.
Some copies read “the power that recognizes” instead of “the power that perceives and directs.”

Either the object of “says” is understood from the context, or the verb means simply “speaks.” The author quotes this report in the opening of the book's section on theology, but leaves out the words from “he says” to “when he enters.”

This follows an Arabic letter-writing form: “From Zayd ibn ʿAmr to Khalid ibn Bakr.” Here, “the Living” lives through the life of the First, and “the Sustainer” sustains through His sustaining power. Neither is an independent being beside Him; there is no partner in God's rule.

The mystic stresses the word “thing,” one of the broadest terms. The point is not that “thing” is simply the most indefinite word, as the grammarian al-Azhari says. Rather, being a thing goes with existing, so “thing” applies broadly to whatever exists.
In short, neither the natural human being nor the soul has unlimited power. Their work is limited to bodies and individual spirits. Only the human being at the intellectual level has universal reach.

“Part of the whole” means that every being is contained within the broad reality of the human being. The simple reality, because it is one, gathers all good and all the levels of existence. The author compares this with the teaching that the purified Imams contain all the souls, spirits, and bodies of the world. Other writers say that all creatures reflect human traits: animals reflect desire, wild beasts anger, ants greed, and other creatures resentment, pride, or vanity. Avicenna says in one of his prefaces, “Praise be to God, who created the human being and created all other worlds from what overflowed from him.” He means that the human being contains something like the heavens, angels, animals, plants, and other things. If you look at the meaning and not just the outward form, you see no difference in God's creation. Your hunger, thirst, greed, desire, joy, and sorrow are like what exists in animals and other beings. The true general ideas and beliefs within you also exist in others like you. The author adds that all things have their source, higher form, and fullest state in the human being, which is why a person may rise above the angels or fall below devils and animals.
The word means “described.” The author links “there is nothing that does not praise Him” with the statement that all beings bow down to God. Both describe the obedience and submission of all things.

The Persian line means, “This first movement was sought from the Eternal Beauty.” The author links this to the report that God created Adam in His image: the human being reflects both God's commands that bring things into being and His commands that guide conduct.
This explains why all those who know God agree on the point.

The author gives several possible meanings. The world may come into being through the unity that reflects God's simple reality, through the totality of God's beautiful names, or through the whole of created beings. On the last reading, “Him” in “the individual realities are nothing but Him” refers to that whole. On the first two readings, it refers to the totality of God's names and their created reflections. In each case, the point is that God is present with the whole and that, without Him, it could bring nothing about. The verse says He is “the fourth” of three, not the third, because God is not one limited being set beside the others. He is not a third item in a set of three. The verse points to God's presence within multiplicity and, by extension, to unity within multiplicity. Mulla Sadra cites the first idea here, though his main discussion concerns unity within multiplicity.

Here “animal power” means the term used by natural philosophers and doctors for the power that expands and contracts the heart and arteries to refresh the body. The author discusses it again two chapters later.

The argument relies on the principle that lower levels can give way to higher ones: plant powers come before animal powers, and animal powers before powers of the soul. If we look at how matter becomes ready over time, the liver comes first; if we look at priority in being and nobility, the brain comes first. The heart's priority is relative to the other organs. The author brings these views together by distinguishing the different ways in which each organ can be said to come first.

The words up to “it is not unlikely” explain why Avicenna says the body is prepared for sensory life. “The organs of the animal are completed with it” means that the sense organs form with the sensory soul, just as plant organs form with the plant soul, whose first power is nourishment. At first, the phrase about animal organs may seem unrelated and even wrong, since every animal organ needs nourishment or it would quickly decay—even nails and hair, which cannot feel touch. The three bodily spirits—natural, animal, and soul-related—are also well known in medical writing. The phrase is meant to stress that the animal's organs form with the sensory soul, while nourishment reaches more organs than sensation does. Avicenna often uses the name of a power's action for the power itself: “nourishment” for the nutritive power, “perception” for the perceiving power, and “movement” for the power that moves.

The author means there are three nutritive powers at issue: the father's own power, a power received from the father, and one that later develops in the child. He does not say it comes from the mother, even though that might seem more likely, because the account says the spirit comes from the father's seed.

An effect needs its cause to keep existing, not only to begin. If a force pushes a stone upward and then stops, but the stone keeps moving upward, we know that the force prepared the motion and another cause now carries it on. Here, the father's soul cannot simply prepare the inherited nutritive power and then leave it to continue by itself. Nor can the power come directly from the Active Source, since the argument concerns the power inherited from the father, not the child's own nutritive power.

This is not true of growth or the four powers that serve nourishment, except in number or in degree as they act on different organs. Growth is simply stretching, whether it happens in a nerve, vein, artery, or other organ. The same is true of drawing in, holding, and expelling. Digestion may differ because it produces different stages of processed food. But the difference does apply to nourishment and reproduction, since each changes the body's material in a different way.

One might ask whether the point the author accepts—that different effects require their sources to differ in number or kind—is enough for his opponent. The author's aim is to deny that the powers are wholly separate. They can differ in the bodily level while existing together in a simpler, more unified way in the soul.

An object's nature does not change depending on what it is compared with. If these powers truly differed in kind, their natures could not become one in the soul. The author's account of difference below and unity above makes sense in terms of existence, not nature: material kinds are distinct, while their existence is gathered into one at the higher level. The wording in the main text is not fully clear.

The causes in the bodily world also have a kind of unity. The powers are ways of existing, and their common features and differences belong to the same reality. They act in one body, come from one soul, and serve one aim.
“Rather” corrects the earlier claim: many effects do not always mean many causes. There may be many causes at a lower level and one cause at a higher level.

Mulla Sadra also uses this rule in The Origin and the Return to argue against a second world existing beside this one. The proof relies on the possibility of the lower level in an ascending series, corresponding to the possibility of the higher in a descending series. It also rules out a jump in the soul's inner development, just as there can be no jump in its change of place.

“Animal power” has more than one meaning. It can refer to the powers of sensation and movement found in animals, or to the power that prepares the organs to receive those abilities. The second meaning is intended here and is common among doctors. They divide the chief organs into the liver, heart, and brain, and the body's spirits into three kinds: natural spirit, which begins in the liver and flows through the veins; animal spirit, which begins in the heart and flows through the arteries; and soul-related spirit, which begins in the brain and flows through the nerves. They also distinguish plant, animal, and rational powers. In their account, animal power manages the vital spirit, expands and contracts the heart and arteries to draw in air and remove smoky vapor, and supports fear, anger, grief, and joy. By circulating vital spirit through the organs, it keeps them alive and prepares them to receive sensation and movement.
What about atrophy, a disease caused by lack of nourishment?

This conflicts with what the author said earlier. There he argued that if powers of sensation and movement were the same as plant powers, plants would sense and move at will. Here, he answers the claim that the powers differ by saying they share a broader class.

This explains how a broader class can also be a distinct kind. A fully grown plant, such as a tree, has settled into its kind and cannot keep developing toward animal life. But a seed or embryo is still developing: its plant life is not yet complete and remains open to higher stages. Its power to grow is therefore a broader class of power, still in the process of becoming a particular kind.

The ability to receive something is not enough by itself; it also needs a power that makes it ready to receive. Animal power is what allows nutritive power to receive the powers of sensation and movement. In the same way, mixed elements need a balanced temperament before they can receive a new form.

The author's statement is very surprising. Animal power prepares the organ to receive sensation and movement; it does not produce them. Their active source is the power associated with the brain. The author himself says this earlier, and the medical tradition agrees.

The doctors' point is that the absence of sensation and movement does not prove that the animal power is gone. They say it still maintains the vital spirit in the paralyzed organ, expands and contracts its arteries, and prepares it to sense and move if paralysis were not in the way.
The wording is faulty. The text should delete either “from” or “from it.”

The author has already considered this objection. The matter itself may not be the obstacle; something in it may block the power, as happens in forced movement. The matter may be ready for a body's natural movement while another factor prevents that movement. One might ask whether the matter is truly ready if it cannot receive the movement's effect. In the author's account, the effect is a weaker form of the power, so matter that receives the power is also ready for its effects. This point does not settle the present case, since it would still allow the power in a paralyzed organ to be one of sensation and movement.
The Arabic sentence begins with “if” but does not complete the conditional. The wording appears to be incomplete.

Here “the unseen realm” includes the higher realm of pure intellect. Otherwise, these inner powers belong to the unseen realm; they are not simply closer to it. They belong to its lower level, not its highest level.

The example actually shows that animals need imagination and memory, though the author means to show why they need the shared inner sense. He may be relying on the close link among these powers. More precisely, imagining is becoming aware of what is stored in the imagination. The shared inner sense can perceive both what comes from outside and what arises within, while imagination keeps that inner image.

This proof is stated loosely. The author has said elsewhere that perception is not a power spread through matter or attached to a material thing. The outer senses and the places linked to inner perception are signs of perception, not the true perceivers. So this passage resembles a proof, but it does not establish the claim on its own. The next chapter supports this point.

“The matter of the qualities felt through touch” means the basic elements that bear them. It may also mean the active and passive qualities. Saying that the body is “of the same kind” means that it shares their general nature. The organ must still be free of the particular quality it senses, as the author explains next. Although the body has a balanced quality, a middle state between two extremes is almost as if it had neither.

One might say that sight senses light, so its organ can be like light. The meeting point of the optic nerves is even called the meeting point of two lights. But how could the organ of hearing be like what it hears? How could it be made of sounds, as the organ of sight is said to be light? The answer is that the hearing organ is like air, which carries sound. The body's matter and its form join as one, and the hearing organ shares the air's clear, open quality. The text's references to something “like transparent material” concern hearing; “or something similar” refers to sight.

This argument seems to apply to the outer senses too. Elsewhere, the author says that the images we perceive—even through touch—are not the same as the physical images that are present outside us. Perhaps “material” here means that a physical organ must be present. These sensory images are less separate from matter than images held in imagination. Some call their realm Hurqalya, a Persian term for the imaginal world or its heavens.
“All bodies” means all the body's parts. Touch can be present in all of them, and it can sense all kinds of elemental bodies, not only vapor or soft material.

The author is repeating a view attributed to Avicenna: some people may not treat touch as one final kind of sense. I do not recall this argument earlier in the book. The author may have discussed it in The Origin and the Return and says he will return to it later.

At first, the rule seems to contradict itself: if the subtle spirit that carries a sense is of the same kind as what it senses, how can it be free of that quality? There is no contradiction. The organ and the sense power must be free of the particular quality, while still sharing its general nature. Their relation is like that between matter and form: matter is free of the form it receives, yet is suited to receive it. The organ of sight must be free of the images it sees, yet share their nature. The one who senses and what is sensed can then come together in perception.

The problem only shows that touch senses a difference in degree. It cannot detect heat if the organ has heat at exactly the same level. The organ's heat must differ: if it is weaker, the difference feels cold; if it is stronger, the sense detects the added heat. Experience confirms this, so there is no contradiction.

“Also” continues the earlier point: “All this...” The idea is that the balance of qualities in an animal's body needs a power to preserve it. The same idea can be applied to plants and other things, or restated as the need for something to preserve each body's form. But this argument is weak: a body's own form can preserve its arrangement and balance for some time. Animals need touch because their bodies are more delicate, their balance is finer, and they are more exposed to harm.

The sentence leaves out “them”: the question is how material things can perceive the forms within them, since those forms are not present to the things themselves. The point concerns how what is perceived is present to the perceiver, not how the perceiver is present to what is perceived.
The author's wording is loose in several ways. These points should be read alongside the earlier discussions of what knows and what is known, and of material and immaterial things.

The sentence means that the elements are not aware because they are divided by opposing qualities and are constantly changing. Opposition keeps one quality from being fully present; constant change also prevents lasting awareness. An animal's body changes too, but its soul is connected to a higher, more unified realm. The author also argues earlier that, if plants had touch, they would need powers of desire and movement and would count as animals.

The main text is discussing awareness through touch. Its argument may suggest that plants and lifeless things have a simple kind of awareness, but that is different from the sense of touch at issue here.

Mulla Sadra gives a fuller answer in The Origin and the Return. One might object that the senses detect opposing qualities, such as heat and cold, not “opposition” itself, which is an idea grasped by reason. Why, then, should the number of touch powers depend on kinds of opposition? Also, sight perceives opposites such as black and white through one power. Why could touch not do the same?

One weak answer is that the basic qualities felt by touch—heat, cold, wetness, and dryness—differ more sharply than colors, smells, and tastes, so touch needs separate powers. The better answer is this: an animal's body has a balanced mixture of these basic qualities. When one of them is opposed by what the body touches, the animal is affected. The balanced state is cold compared with pure heat and hot compared with pure cold; it is wet compared with pure dryness and dry compared with pure wetness. So the power of touch can be counted as four powers, one for each way the body can be affected by an opposing quality. It is not necessary to count separate powers for every related difference, such as rough and smooth or hard and soft. Those are effects of the basic qualities, and counting them separately would lead to far more than four. The point is that touch responds to what opposes the body's balanced state, not to qualities that match it.
The objection does not settle the question. Why could the odor not be stirred up by the change caused by rubbing and vaporizing?
This, too, is not conclusive. The apple might wilt because the surrounding air repeatedly strikes it, just as air around an object can dry it out.
That is, heat the camphor until it becomes vapor and its whole substance disappears. The word “until” here means that the heating brings about this result.

“It” means the scented substance. First, vaporize the camphor; then spread the same amount of it through many different places by carrying it there, without further heating. The first process uses up more substance but produces a weaker smell; the second uses almost no additional substance yet produces a stronger smell. Here, “vapor” means the odor, and “vaporizing” means giving the air a quality.

What is carried onward is the air's quality, not the air itself. Striking or pulling something away makes the air ripple. The air that moves then draws the air beside it into the same movement. These ripples and changing qualities pass from one stretch of air to the next until they reach air that no longer follows them.

The argument is circular: it says that transmission causes hearing because sound travels, but sound's travel is what it needs to prove. A circular argument gives us only probability, not the certainty this question requires. As Fakhr al-Din al-Razi notes in discussing how rippling air produces sound, strong intuition may sometimes make it feel certain.

Today, natural philosophers and mathematicians have made deep studies of hearing, sight, and the other outer senses, supported by extensive experiments. Their valuable findings can help resolve some of the problems raised here and should be consulted in a fuller examination of these questions.

The person raising this objection should first ask how air ripples and takes on a shape. He seems not to have understood it, perhaps imagining that air takes the shape of letters as writing takes shape on a page. That is why he raised this objection. The rippling is more like the waves made when a stone is dropped into water; the changing quality is more like water taking on different colors in succession. For example, when someone says the Arabic word ḍaraba (“he struck”), the air ripples outward in circles, like water around a stone. As the speaker says the first sound, the air around them takes on that sound's quality, as water might turn yellow; with the next sound it takes on another quality, as if turning green; and with the last, another, as if turning red. These changing qualities spread around the speaker. The whole ripple and its quality cannot reach one person but only part of it reach another, since a quality cannot be divided in this way.

The very feature that seems to cause the problem also resolves it. Air takes on the letters in succession. Sound and speech do not persist unchanged. If the air held each letter as writing holds a shape on a page, the likeness of all its parts would indeed be a problem. But sound is not fixed either as it begins or as it continues. Each part of the similar air takes on each letter in turn. In this account, hearing does not repeat. If the air around you is warmed by your breath, then quickly cooled and returned to its usual state, does everyone nearby feel the heat over and over? No: the warmth has already vanished by the time it reaches touch. The same goes for the cold and the return to normal temperature. Apply this to the successive sounds ḍ, r, and b in ḍarb. One might object that, since there is no indivisible instant, the air's first quality lasts for some time, so each new arrival of air should make hearing repeat. But air is continuous: one part blocks another from arriving all at once, just as hearing cannot be divided into separate acts. Or, if we allow the point for the sake of argument, each quality in one stretch of air may prepare the neighboring stretch to take on the next quality. The preparation comes and goes as the new quality appears.

No one holds that the same parcel of air travels all the way from the striker to the struck object and then to the ear; this is only a far-fetched possibility. The air released by the strike at one end of a long distance cannot cut through all the air between there and the ear. The note may instead point to what we said: one stretch of air prepares the next to take on the quality, so that the quality reaches the ear without the original air itself traveling there.

The view chosen by the author is strong and avoids the difficulties about hearing direction, nearness, and distance. It also accounts for cases that challenge the other account: people hear outside sounds with their heads under water, and can hear a stick striking the side of a water-filled basin. Ringing in the head comes from movement of inner vapors and air. We have already seen that the evidence from sound traveling in air does not prove that rippling causes sound or that transmission causes hearing. This view could also make sense of reports that Pythagoras and others heard sounds from the heavenly spheres. Still, the third and fifth pieces of evidence given earlier seem to require transmission through air. Perhaps there is another hidden condition, or some obstacle such as air that is too thin or too dense.

The position need not involve contact in the same way for every sense. Powers differ in subtlety and in how far they rise above matter and mixture with it. The spatial conditions they require differ accordingly. This answers the objection that touch and taste involve contact even though what they perceive is not material: what they perceive must touch the sense organ.
This is only an example. On this view, the subtle body between the sound and the organ might be water, or it might be a heavenly sphere.

The argument uses one word, “power,” in both of its meanings at once. This is generally disallowed by writers on logic and language. Here the two meanings are the capacity to be affected and the ability to act.

An editor objects that this account is made less likely by the fact that we sometimes hear sounds incorrectly; there is no sense in saying that the external sound itself is mistaken. The sounds we hear are also approximate rather than exact.

The objection also applies to touch. As explained earlier, touch does not perceive the direction from which something came, yet what it senses is not universal. A sound, too, has particular features besides its direction. The reply is that, while touch may not perceive the direction from which a touched thing came, it does perceive the direction of the body part that carries the sense of touch. So its object is not universal.

If hearing first perceives a nearby sound and only later, by tracing the waves, a distant one, it would perceive the same sound as both near and far. If it does not perceive the sound at the ear and has not yet traced it back to its distance, then it first hears a sound without any place or direction and so hears a universal sound. That is impossible. It would also fail to perceive the other details that make the sound particular. If it cannot perceive where the air carrying the sound is, then it cannot perceive the direction of the sound's source either.

Even if the premises of this argument were proved with certainty, it would show only that a higher level of existence contains what is found in a lower one—for example, intellect and the imaginal realm contain what is found in the bodily realm. It would not prove that one body contains every perfection found in another body, even if one body is subtler and more refined than the other. In any case, the argument offered here is not a proof.

I say: the view he chose about sight is a powerful one, with sound insight, and well suited to teaching and learning. Yet what the Shaykh of Illumination, al-Suhrawardi, says is also lofty and precious. It points to the soul's highest states. He explicitly says that souls are pure lights without a fixed essence, because they never stop rising beyond each level they reach. Their existence has no boundary at which it comes to rest.

An essence is what can be bounded by a definition that includes what belongs to it and excludes what does not. It expresses a limit in existence, if existence can be limited. The author's path concerns the perceiver's union with what is directly perceived; the Shaykh's path concerns its union with what is perceived indirectly. The latter is included in the former. Union with what is directly perceived entails union with what is indirectly perceived, since things enter the mind as they are. Their essence is the same in both realms, while existence is both what distinguishes them and what they share. A single reality is multiplied only when something else, of whatever kind, intervenes between its instances.

Illuminationist knowledge can also be stronger or weaker. The soul's knowledge of itself, its powers, and its body is all direct and present knowledge, since all of them are present to it as a thing is present to itself. This means simply that a thing is never separate from itself, though this presence can vary in strength. Even when the soul forgets its Lord and is made to forget itself, its knowledge of itself remains present knowledge. When it comes to know itself and thereby knows its Lord, that too is present knowledge. But what a difference there is between those two states!

How could the soul fail to know things through an illuminating relation, when pure existence is the basis of the perceiver's own existence? Every being has what it is in, why it is, what it is, and whether it is. In the divine section of The Four Journeys, while explaining the saying “The perfection of knowing Him is to affirm Him,” the author says that anyone who understands the meaning of Necessary Existence—as the fullest and most complete existence, on which all possible beings with their incomplete natures depend—also understands that there must be a Necessary Existent. If there were not, nothing in the world would exist. But that conclusion is false, so its premise must be false as well. The truth of existence is known fully through direct, witnessing knowledge, because, as we established earlier, the image of a thing in knowledge must itself be the reality of the thing known.
The author appears to limit direct, present knowledge to two cases, but that is only when the question is viewed broadly. The objections against the Shaykh can be answered.

The first objection is answered by saying that what is material in relation to the first principles is not material in relation to those principles. The author himself cites the learned Mirdamad to this effect in the discussion of forms in the First Journey. The same can be said of the soul, considered from its hidden and more inward level.
The second objection is answered by the Shaykh's suggestion that one of the images exists in the imaginal world. That is a reasonable view, but the author gives no reason for dismissing it.

The third objection is answered by noting that the author's claim—that perception is only an image of a thing being present to the perceiver—requires a particular relation between them. This is contradicted by our knowledge of ourselves, where everyone agrees that knower and known are one. It is also contradicted by cases in which the author, Porphyry, and others say that the knower becomes one with what it knows. The soul has another kind of unity as well.
The fourth objection is answered by what we have said about the name “illuminating relation.”

I have discussed this at length even though it goes beyond the scope of these notes, because the author rejects this view in many of his works, including The Four Journeys, The Throne of Wisdom, and his notes on The Wisdom of Illumination. I have found the view true, and so I have not concealed it. I have lifted some of its veils and brought out a few of its secrets, on the condition that you keep them from those who should not hear them. God is witness between you and me.

The principles proved in the higher study of the intellect and what it understands show that the thing perceived is an image free of matter, and that it is perceived by the immaterial soul. But this does not remove the need for natural inquiry into the connection between the bodily power rooted in the body and external matter. Experience shows that perception is connected to the body and to external material things. So the questions of how an image is imprinted or how rays leave the eye still need to be studied, even after we establish that the image perceived is immaterial.

As explained earlier, saying that sight and the other senses produce a knowing image in the soul does not remove the need to study how material sensation occurs—that is, how a bodily power interacts with external matter. So the author's argument against the theories of imprinting and rays, based only on the claim that perception belongs to the soul, does not refute either theory.
